output.title: Focus blocks come after the workflow decision
output.body:
Before you protect a “focus block,” decide what is actually stealing the focus.

For a small business owner, the useful question is not whether AI sounds smart. It is whether one recurring task keeps interrupting the day: repeated customer questions, invoice data entry, or lead follow-up. If it is the same kind of work showing up again and again, that is a workflow. If it changes every time, it is probably not the first thing to automate. That distinction matters more than the tool.

A simple check: does the task follow a pattern, repeat weekly, and have a clear input and output? If yes, it is worth measuring before you spend time trying to “make room” for automation. If no, keep it manual and move on. No spreadsheet heroics required; a plain week of notes is usually enough to tell you whether you are dealing with a process or just a busy Tuesday.

That is the bounded decision Bareni starts with: identify one recurring workflow, then decide whether it should stay manual, be shared with a hire, or be scoped for automation. Bareni’s normal sequence is to identify the workflow honestly, say whether AI fits, and then define a pilot scope if it does. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

The first move is simple: name the one task, time how often it interrupts your week, and check whether it repeats in a pattern before you protect the block.
